newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Q3 GDP eases but inventories provide lift.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Q3 GDP eases but inventories provide lift.

text.p: Easing consumption, exports and government spending defined a marked moderation in third quarter U.S. Gross Domestic Product (GDP) to a level seen sustainable through year-end, economists said.
Inventory rebuilding pushed the preliminary read beyond most economists' expectations, however, portending a renewed consumer appetite in the fourth quarter.

"The degree of inventory accumulation is very pronounced," said Michael Niemira, economist at Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi. "(Inventories) were a little higher than expected and consequently so was the overall GDP number."
"The composition of the data will be very different," Niemira said. "We have seen some softness in manufacturing, which probably has already reflected an inventory correction."

Joseph Liro, chief economist at CIBC Wood Gundy Securities Corp, said the 2.2 percent rate is positive for the economy and the markets. The rate of growth coupled with the absence of inflation is remarkable, he added.

"It's increasingly looking like the notion that we're in a brave new world is in fact true," he said. "We have gone 5.5 years in the business cycle where growth hasn't been shabby, but without generating any inflation pressures."
Liro said the inventory overhang is not so big as to restrain the economy into the fourth quarter.
Dissecting the sales component, Steve Ricchiuto, chief financial economist, BZW Securities, noted the final sales number was low but perhaps not so weak as it appears.
"Final sales for domestic purchases were stronger at 1.2 percent," Ricchiuto said. "What happen here really was a big expansion in the trade deficit."
Ricchiuto added "the trade deficit ballooned out to $132.2 billion from $114.7 billion...imports ballooned the deficit and a lot of that wound up in inventory."
Niemira said he questioned whether the 0.6 percent rise in exports is representative of the trend. He said the number will likely strengthen to establish a 3.0 percent to 4.0 percent range.
"We may be just correcting for the stronger second quarter pace of exports," he said.
David Sloan, senior economist at I.D.E.A. Inc, said the inventories were, in part, involuntary and together with weak components presents a less encouraging fourth quarter picture.
"Some of the inventory was involuntary given that final sales were weak," Sloan said, adding that it was also partly stockpiling for a possible General Motors strike.

Still, surprises in the report were few and Sloan said fourth quarter GDP estimates should present growth similar to the third quarter. Like Niemira, Sloan said fourth quarter GDP should grow at a 2.0 percent rate.
